extracted.intended_audience: fans, researchers and practitioners of British television comedy (comedians, producers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for the format, rounds, casting and content norms of a topical British satirical panel show (exemplified by Mock the Week). Useful for producers, performers, and researchers designing or evaluating similar programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall format emphasis (topical satire over quiz)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quiz aspect of answering questions relating to major and regional news items ... is sidelined to focus on satirical, topical discussions on news items, stand-up routines, and the use of improvisational comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the programme maintained a quiz aspect, it was largely sidelined completely with a focus on comedy derived from topical, satirical discussions on the subject of each question, as well as from rounds featuring either stand-up routines by certain panellists, or improvisation comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team composition and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Two teams of three panelists each, all comedians, compete over four rounds, presided over by a host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike similar programmes, the format did not use team captains or maintain a proper scoring system – teams generally win a round depending on who Dara, the host, deemed won it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode editing and runtime constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Each episode on the BBC was edited to include about four rounds from those filmed, to fit a 30-minute timeslot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some content not used was often retained for use in a compilation episode, which also included outtakes and highlights. The TLC revival introduced an extended runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions and subjects are taken from news items made during the week before an episode's filming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rounds and jokes are based on current events (topical) — the programme focuses on satirical, topical discussion rather than factual quizzing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture of the Week round — comedic identification and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: An image round in which panelists are shown a photograph from a news item and must identify the related story from it; the round usually focuses on panelists giving comedic answers that are deliberately wrong or mock the subject(s) of the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The in-joke is Hugh Dennis finally saying the obvious answer. The round generally does not conclude when the obvious answer is given, as both the host and panelists will usually enter topical, satirical discussion on the news item, including any additional questions given by the host.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wheel of News (stand-up challenge) — themed stand-up on random topics
rubrics_metrics.description: A stand-up challenge in which a handful of panelists must perform a stand-up routine, with each basing it on a subject determined by a 'Random Topic Generator' (e.g. Education).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The host often introduces the round with a title that is a comical reference to a recent event. Initially featured most panelists; number was gradually reduced to two to provide more time for routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: If This is the Answer, What is the Question? — reverse-question improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists are given the answer to a question on a topic and attempt to reveal what the question is, related to a current news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The round usually involves panellists giving comedic questions that the answer could be connected to, and continues until the host prompts one member to give the correct question. The round generally does not conclude when this happens, as both the host and panelists will usually enter topical, satirical discussion on the news item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headliners — abbreviation-based gag guessing
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists are shown a photograph relating to a current news story, with the addition of a four-letter abbreviation for a four-word story headline relating to the photo; panelists give comedic responses of what the abbreviation stands for until the host prompts them to guess the correct answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'BRNS' = 'Blair Retires Next Summer'; 'TFHC' = 'Tories Fight Hospital Cuts'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes We'd Like to See — rapid-fire improvisational prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvisation round similar to 'Scenes from a Hat' in which panelists are given two topics and must provide comedic suggestions and ideas for each one, with the host buzzing each panelist after they give an idea to let another come forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example topics: 'Commercials That Never Made it to Air', 'Rejected Questions From This Year's Exams', 'What the Queen Didn't Say in Her Annual Message'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsreel (Film Dub style) — silent footage dubbing
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvisation round in which a panellist is shown a piece of news footage with no sound, and must provide either a comedic commentary track, or vocal track of the people involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primarily performed by Hugh Dennis in the series; often included in compilation or special episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Between the lines — 'translator' political improv
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvisation round involving two panellists: one performs as a notable figure conducting a press conference, while another acts as a 'translator', comically stating what they 'really' mean to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: panellist A as the Prime Minister says 'We are making certain that schools are well provided with school meals', panellist B translates comically as 'We made a deal for cheap soup and biscuits from the Russians.' Since the 2026 revival this has appeared more regularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: You Think That's Bad? — anecdote escalation (TLC revival)
rubrics_metrics.description: A round where the panelists tell short anecdotes and try to outdo each other in tales of woe; the host then decides who has the worst anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced in the TLC version as a new round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting criterion — comedians skilled in stand-up and improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Panellists were primarily comedians, including stand-up comedians, many of whom made multiple appearances; regular, frequent, occasional or one-off guest panellists during the show's history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hugh Dennis appeared in every BBC episode; the format expects participants able to perform stand-up routines, quick topical jokes, and improvisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content risk and complaints standard (edginess vs. offence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The show has been the source of complaints due to risqué comments made by panellists and the show's extreme use of profanity; BBC ruled some jokes 'humiliating' and 'risked offending the audience'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Frankie Boyle's controversial lines led to challenge and criticism. The production team and broadcaster may limit risqué material to avoid complaints; Frankie Boyle later claimed producers were 'afraid of frightening the horses'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and representation concern (guest selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lack of female guests on the programme has been the subject of complaints; commentators criticised the male-dominated genre and treatment of some performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jo Brand and others noted discomfort with the competitive/aggressive tendency; casting choices have been publicly critiqued and can affect reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series revival and format evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Revival on TLC introduced extended runtime, new rounds, and changes in regular panellists; format evolved over time with many early rounds abolished and a smaller set of primary rounds dominating episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a three-year absence the series was revived for TLC with extended runtime; some rounds reintroduced or made more regular (e.g., 'Between the lines'), and casting/regularity of panellists changed (Hugh Dennis no longer in every episode).
